answer.label: Not Marilyn Monroe — a 1920s joke of uncertain origin
answer.authorDates: Eugenics joke, origin uncertain · in print by 7 December 1923
answer.sourceLine: This is a travelling anecdote, not a Monroe line. The earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗ ran in the Boston Globe of 7 December 1923 — in print before Marilyn Monroe was born — and the speakers were Anatole France and Isadora Duncan. The same joke was later retold about George Bernard Shaw and Duncan (which Shaw denied in writing in 1926), about Einstein and a chorus girl (1953), and finally about Arthur Miller and Monroe, which Quote Investigator traces no further back than a 2009 Daily Mail book review that itself called the story “probably apocryphal”. In that Monroe version the punchline is Miller’s; hers is the set-up line.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Floating anecdote — no verified original speaker
“Editorial Points”, Boston Globe, 7 December 1923 — Anatole France and Isadora Duncan
Shaw & Duncan (1925) · Shaw & an unnamed foreign actress (1931) · Shaw & a Zürich lady (1942) · Einstein & a chorus girl (1953)
Traced by Quote Investigator no further back than a Daily Mail review of 27 March 2009, which called it “probably apocryphal”

source.excerpt: In all probability the conversation between Isadore Duncan and Anatole France, who were discussing eugenics, came to a sudden stop when Isadore said: “Imagine a child with my beauty and your brains!” and Anatole responded: “Yes, but imagine a child with my beauty and your brains!”
trail: The earliest documented instance is an Editorial Points squib in the Boston Globe of 7 December 1923, with Isadora Duncan proposing and Anatole France answering Quote Investigator’s chain ↗. A Shaw-and-Duncan version was circulating in the same years, told as an exchange of letters at a New York interfraternity conference in 1925.

Shaw denied it. In a letter dated 3 March 1926 he wrote that the Italian journalist had invented the dancer and her proposal and stolen the witty reply, adding that “99% of these stories are flat falsehoods”. In 1931, in Sewell Stokes’s Hear the Lions Roar, he claimed the reply as his own but insisted the proposer was a foreign actress, not Isadora both statements ↗.

His biographer Hesketh Pearson gave the same story in 1942 with an anonymous woman in Zürich, and wrote that it had been foisted on to Isadora Duncan, who was not the lady. Wikiquote’s Duncan page carries the Shaw exchange too, with an editorial note that the earliest form its editors have found is in 10,000 Jokes, Toasts & Stories (1939), where the proposer is again unidentified Wikiquote ↗.

Marilyn Monroe enters last. Quote Investigator’s only Monroe instance is a Daily Mail review of 27 March 2009 covering Jeffrey Meyers’s The Genius and the Goddess, and the reviewer labelled the anecdote “probably apocryphal”. Monroe died in 1962; the joke was in print before she was born her dates ↗.
source.excerptNote: The spelling ‘Isadore’ is the newspaper’s. This is the earliest instance Quote Investigator located, and it already reads as a joke in circulation rather than a reported conversation — note the hedge, ‘in all probability’. The punchline here belongs to Anatole France; every later celebrity to whom it has been credited, Marilyn Monroe included, arrived afterwards.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the popular one-line wording, because it corresponds to no identified published text — it is a smoothed composite of a joke that has been retold in different words for a century. The specific passage excerpted here, from the Boston Globe of 7 December 1923, was published well before 1931 and is in the public domain in the United States. The later renderings are not cleared: Sewell Stokes’s 1931 book, Hesketh Pearson’s 1942 biography and Jeffrey Meyers’s 2009 book remain in copyright to their authors, estates and publishers, and the US status of the 1953 Drew Pearson newspaper column depends on a copyright renewal we have not verified. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Marilyn Monroe
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Monroe
author.bio: Marilyn Monroe (born Norma Jeane Mortenson, 1 June 1926; died 4 August 1962) was married to the playwright Arthur Miller from 1956 to 1961 — a pairing the press reduced to ‘the genius and the goddess’, which is exactly the shape this joke needs. She is also one of the internet’s biggest attractors of orphaned quotations: Wikiquote’s own editors warn that quotes are routinely misattributed to Monroe on social media and in self-help book images. A beauty-versus-brains gag about a hypothetical child lands on her almost by gravity — but the joke was decades old before she ever met Miller.

copyAttribution: "But suppose the child inherited my beauty and your brains?" — not Marilyn Monroe. Its origin is uncertain: it is a eugenics joke whose earliest documented instance is the Boston Globe of 7 December 1923, where the speakers were Anatole France and Isadora Duncan. It was later retold about George Bernard Shaw (who denied the Duncan story in 1926, though he claimed the reply itself in 1931), about Einstein and a chorus girl in 1953, and about Arthur Miller and Monroe only in a 2009 book review that called the story probably apocryphal — and there the retort is Miller's, not hers.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is not a quotation with a wandering author so much as a joke with a casting couch. The template is fixed — beauty proposes, brains demurs — and famous couples have been dropped into it for a century.

items.why: The Monroe telling that Quote Investigator located dates from 27 March 2009, in a Daily Mail review of Jeffrey Meyers’s The Genius and the Goddess, and the reviewer immediately called it “probably apocryphal”. In that version Monroe supplies the proposal and Arthur Miller supplies the retort the chain ↗.

In a letter of 3 March 1926 Shaw wrote that no beautiful American dancer had ever proposed marriage to him on eugenic or any other grounds, and that the journalist had invented the dancer and stolen the witty reply. In 1931 he told Sewell Stokes he had made the reply — but to a foreign actress whose name he had forgotten both statements ↗.

items.who: A 1953 newspaper column, opposite a chorus girl
items.why: A ‘Washington Merry-Go-Round’ column by Drew Pearson, printed 9 November 1953, has a chorus girl propose to Einstein and Einstein reply about children with his looks and her brains — the same joke, thirty years on, with new casting 1953 citation ↗.

items.who: No documented source uses this exact sentence
items.why: The 1923 Boston Globe has “Yes, but imagine a child with my beauty and your brains!”; a 1928 syndicated column has “Yes, but supposing it had your brains and my beauty!”; Hesketh Pearson’s 1942 biography has “What if the child inherits my body and your brains?” The popular one-line form is a smoothed composite, not a transcript the variants ↗.

Wikiquote’s editors warn on her page that quotes are routinely misattributed to Monroe on social media and in self-help book images; the beauty-and-brains anecdote is not among her sourced quotations there Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: A eugenics joke of uncertain origin, earliest documented instance 7 December 1923, where the speakers were Anatole France and Isadora Duncan — and pinned on Marilyn Monroe only decades after her death the evidence ↗.

context.heading: A joke with a slot for a famous name
lead: The structure never changes: a celebrated beauty proposes a child to a celebrated brain, and the brain replies that the genes might come out the other way round. Only the casting changes. Between 1923 and 2009 the parts were played by Anatole France and Isadora Duncan, George Bernard Shaw and Duncan, Shaw and an unnamed foreign actress, Shaw and an anonymous woman in Zürich, Albert Einstein and a chorus girl, and finally Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe — the whole chain is laid out by Quote Investigator ↗.

Shaw, who was the joke’s most durable host, addressed it twice. In a letter of 3 March 1926 he flatly denied the Duncan story and blamed an Italian journalist for inventing it. Five years later he told the writer Sewell Stokes something more equivocal: that he really had made the reply, but to a foreign actress whose name he had forgotten — not to Isadora. His friend and biographer Hesketh Pearson repeated the anonymous-woman version in 1942 and added that the tale had been “foisted on to Isadora Duncan, who was not the lady”. Quote Investigator leaves that branch open: it concludes that the Shaw–Duncan anecdote is apocryphal but the origin of the joke is uncertain, and that Shaw may genuinely have coined the punchline in reply to a woman in Zürich — a letter that has never been found — or may instead have reused a pre-existing remark of anonymous origin.
context.detailsSummary: Why the Monroe version is the weakest link in the chain
detailsBody: The Miller–Monroe telling is the last recorded arrival, not the origin. Quote Investigator’s earliest instance of it is a Daily Mail review of Jeffrey Meyers’s 2009 book The Genius and the Goddess: Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe, published on 27 March 2009 — and the reviewer flagged it as “probably apocryphal” in the same breath as retelling it.

There is also a casting error in how the line now circulates. In every documented version, including the Monroe one, the beauty makes the proposal and the brain delivers the punchline. Attributing ‘But suppose the child inherited my beauty and your brains?’ to Monroe hands her the wrong half of the exchange.
